### 2026-10-25 – Day 2: WORK

**6.5h**

Day 2: WORK

All week I have barely been putting in work, so today was full of cramming.

Hour 0-1.5:
I started out by fully defining what my project was to do. In the beginning, I wanted it to be able to do outputs and inputs. I play the violin, so my idea was that the project should be able to take what I play, find the frequencies, and tell me if it is conforming to how the piece was written. I had to think for a while about what I really wanted, and I tried to think about stuff I always had problems with playing teh violin. One was defintly the difficulty (no duh), but I can't reallychange that. Another was not being able to really understand the piece  and how it was supposed to sound. Sure, I could look up a performance of it, but it was inconvinient, because when you are practicing, you want to iterating the tempo of the piece. A lot of pieces sound really goofy too slow or fast, so I would never really know what it was supposed to sound like when practicing.

That was really what sparked my idea - after a good 1 hour of thinking. (PS: this journal entry was made late and did span the same work session as the TimeLapse, but i forgot to add it to the same entry :)) Lots of thanks to MuseScore, because they let you play your piece at different volumes and tempos, so they partially helped me come up with the idea, though I remebered them after coming up the concept. I dunno maybe it was like subconciously inspired.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/b7f93df9c4d045d1c10accb51dfdc7832f39f3ea9f70f2652733792f5ab256d6.png)
(the play button lets you listen, and the BPM is beats per minute, or the tempo changer thing)

After coming up with the idea, I realized how humunguos of a concept this really is. My machine was supposed to intake a file (at the time I was optimistic and thought it could read a pdf or smth, butnow I realize that probably involves machine learning, which is a big nono for a week project done in a weekend), be able to understand all of the onscure things on the page, and provide coherent audio to help the listener understand what the heck was actually happening. On top of that, I wanted to use the KV-039 audio module I got for the PCB week, and repurpose it (after building week 1 ofc) to be ABLE TO UNDERSTAND THE USER's PLAYING. I don't know what I was thinking, bc that requires way too much coding, and I don't know Python. My most coding experiance is making a freaking cat move in Scratch.mit.edu ( i love scratch tho, no hate).

I slimmed my project down real good. First I scrapped the end part. I took out the whole chunk about me making a user input to the system and the system grading it. I changed this machine to be solely for listening and practising with. Then I worked on changing the accepted file type. I found the MIDI file (GODSEND). This made it so that I did not need to use a freaking PDF and have the computer program analyze it (i do not want my raspberry pi blowing up), and instead the MIDI file uses the notes, and gives them different data values, along with the measures, and stuff like that, and these can be understood with a little bit of coding to audio unpackers

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/e53352896f23c42adb7d3c27f152241b9aa3a41860acbe417b257b9545fad33f.png)
(Lowkey, Gemini explains it better than I ever could)

Finall, looking back on the project, I feared I slimmed it down too much (I definitly did not, but oh well) so I added leds to blink at every beat and measure.

Hour 1.5-3: Part Search:

This hour was decently chill, as I was a mainly just comparing deals, window shopping at Digikey (too expensive for my budget), and deciding what parts I wanted. I ranked what I needed to be good quality to least, and I had my microcontroller at top, audio module next, speakers, display, rotary dial (for tempo), and LEDS at the last place (who needs good quality LEDS am I right?).

For the microcontroller, I was debating wheter to use my Raspberry Pi 2 Model B or my Arduino Elegoo Uno. The Raspberry Pi 2 was a great choice because it had easy power connection and data trasfer (both through microUSB, while Arduino had seperate wires for the two tasks, and both are elusive) and powerful processing. However, the Arduino Elegoo had it's own beenfits like being extremly compatible with electronic components, having a multitude of GPIO pins and being relatively more simple to deal with. I decided to go with the Raspberry Pi 2 after deliberation because I was going to be using the Arduino in my Week 7 project. Also, I took a look at all of teh speciifcations on the Raspberry Pi shop (honestly not great bc it is like 7 years old, but oh well)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/b33d06683bb72c8f8bac84ae379d071f7afc69487ca109df4cab7f74747e8da7.png)
(sry 11 years since release)

Then I looked into my audio compiler. It couldnot be too fancy because too much money and the Raspberry Pi can only handle 1 GB of RAM, but if it was too cheap, it would make the music sound bad, and lag the system. I found the MAX98357, which was a audio compiler with a screw terminal so it can direclty connect to the wires of the speaker. It is not too expensive (even of DigiKey), so I got it on AliExpress bc they the GOAT with their prices.

Display time! I went for the 1.3 Inch OLED IIC Serial White OLED Display Module. The 1.3 inches means you probably wont have to be squinting at it the entire time you're practicing, and the balc background makes the contrast really good. Also, I found one cheap with 4 buttons already attached to it, so I decided to get it so i could have stuff like pause and scrolling through the sound library without having more components.

I had to really look into the specs of both of these items because both of them had to be low power. As I stated in the earlier part, I needed a sound library to store sounds, because otherwise, your computer is much better (honestly the comouetr is better, I just want to make myself feel better). These were a tigght fit, so I hope there is no bottlenecking, but I am not sure (fingers crossed!)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/20cc8c0e9412619f0902e9e23077d9e718a5153106d2d544ad7fe2fbd360dffe.png)

Hour 3-5: CAD

This hour was all about designing an enclosure for my project. I had to start by determining sizes for my enclosure.

First, I had to measure my Raspberry Pi 2, and I could not find the best measurements online because the official sites were really only showing the measurements for the Raspberry Pi 3 and 3+ (only later did I learn that they did have them for the Pi 2, because the dimensions are the same as the 3). For that reason, I did all of the measurements myself!

![WIN_20261025_18_31_47_Pro](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/356e11cc017ef43adb00d7a0f1b8f13df5faf34f282213fb8667f3b9860073b3.jpg)
(I got this like 7 years ago, so it has some wear and tear, but it will do)

So, first I had to measure the entire body. This did not take long, and I got those measurements pretty quickly. Then I measured the holes. This was tricky. The only ruler I have in my house is one of those beat-up wooden rulers with the metal edge, so it can't line up flush with anything to make accurate measurements. After a while of searching online, because that metal edge was really sharp and scratching away at my top layer of the Pi, I discovered the right hole diameter. Then I got the distance from 1 hole to another to get the mounting dimensions.

I started CADing now. I started with the lid. On a side note, I am making the enclosure as a box, with all of the things the user interacts with on the lid. On the lid, we have the display, speakers, rotary dial, and LEDs. This was a doozy. I needed to figure out all of the dimensions, especially the ones from AliExpress (all of them :)). This was especially tricky because it was from AliExpress. Since AliExpress is not the most reliable company, a lot of their products do not have datasheets; therefore, I have no clue about their dimensions. Thankfully, the site provided dimensions for my display and audio unit, but only the dimensions of the entire thing, not the holes or the holes' distance from the edges. After some calculations, I received an estimate, put it into Onshape, and was met with the freaking red flags everywhere because it did not conform to the correct dimensions. I basically gave up on eyeballing it and asked Gemini to do it for me, so if the casing doesn't work, imma blame them :).

CADding after that was really easy, actually. Since the rotary encoder and speaker were both circular, AliExpress just gave their diameter, which i entered as a hole. The plan is just to superglue the sides together and hope for the best.

The LEDs were also really easy, because I just made 2 small holes for them; the plan is just to thread an LED through both holes and have the resistor and stuff dangling down there.

![Screenshot 2026-10-24 184809](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/33c9e76c4c588b80437f1b121bd5ca5d7a1681b1e691202da6aad427b9167552.png)

 Then I worked on the stuff for the bottom box. The box was going to hold the Raspberry Pi, audio module, and all of the wires and its mess. Simple stuff, really, since I had all of the dimensions (that part def took the longest). I made the box, then realized I didn't make a way for the box to connect to the lid (U may see that the lid has indents for the box to lock into - that was made after what I am saying). I made these little protrusions to mesh with the lid, so that worked out. Then I noticed that the little soldered stuff at the bottom of the Raspberry Pi would get in the way of the plastic, so I made built-in standoffs to raise it off the floor of the box a bit. Then, I just checked if they meshed together, and I was done for today!
